bib.title: Teaching models to express their uncertainty in words

question: Can a GPT-3 model be finetuned to state, in words or numbers, a calibrated confidence in its own answers, and does that calibration hold under distribution shift?
hypothesis: Pre-trained models will need to be finetuned to produce calibrated verbalized probabilities, and GPT-3 already has latent representations correlated with its epistemic uncertainty that finetuning can surface.
contributions: CalibratedMath, a suite of 21 arithmetic tasks for testing calibration under distribution shift
GPT-3 can learn to express calibrated uncertainty using words (verbalized probability), in and out of distribution
Calibration is not explained by learning to output logits or by simple heuristics
Comparison to finetuning the model logits (indirect logit)

method.summary: GPT-3 davinci (175B) answers arithmetic questions zero-shot with greedy decoding; answers are held fixed. It is finetuned with supervised learning to append a confidence (a number or one of five words) whose label is GPT-3's empirical accuracy on that question's sub-task. Calibration is scored on held-out task groups with MSE (Brier) and MAD, against logit-based confidences and a constant baseline.
method.task: calibration of verbalized confidence in arithmetic question answering

datasets.name: CalibratedMath Add-subtract
datasets.source: programmatically generated arithmetic questions; GPT-3 zero-shot answers
datasets.preprocessing: label = floor(100*p_T) for numbers, or one of five words by 0.2-wide accuracy interval; random names (john, sam, matt, dan, tom) used instead of ordered words

datasets.name: CalibratedMath Multi-answer
datasets.source: questions with multiple correct answers (e.g. name any prime below 56)

datasets.name: CalibratedMath Multiply-divide
datasets.source: unique-answer multiplication, division, modulo, percentages, fractions

other.smaller_models_tried: GPT-J and 7B GPT-3, too weak at arithmetic

training.objective: supervised finetuning on the confidence token(s); verbalized: match sub-task empirical accuracy; indirect logit: cross-entropy on True/False correctness
training.lr: OpenAI finetuning API default with learning_rate_multiplier = 0.1
training.regularisation: early stopping around n = 2700 examples, chosen when per-sample MSE on the training set stops decreasing

other.api_defaults: other hyperparameters are the OpenAI fine-tuning API defaults, not stated

inference.decoding: greedy for answers and confidence in main results; Expected Value decoding (weighted sum over top five tokens) in few-shot and some appendix runs
inference.samples: one greedy answer per question; few-shot: k examples resampled randomly per query, k from 1 to 50
inference.prompting: Q/A/Confidence format; few-shot uses k random Add-subtract examples with target probabilities

parameters.MAD_bins: K bins with equal numbers of samples, K not stated

metrics.name: MSE
metrics.definition: E_q[(p_M - I(a_M))^2], Brier score of the stated probability against answer correctness

metrics.name: MAD
metrics.definition: mean over K equal-count bins of |acc(b_i) - conf(b_i)|

baselines: constant baseline (best constant on train by MSE)
eval.protocol: single run, no seeds or confidence intervals reported; model answers held fixed, only calibration scored

availability.data: CalibratedMath described in Appendix A / Table 3; no release link in text

results.claim: Finetuned verbalized numbers beat answer logit and constant baseline in MSE on Multi-answer after training on Add-subtract.
results.setup: GPT-3 175B, trained on Add-subtract, evaluated on Multi-answer, greedy decoding
results.table: Table 1, row Verbalized numbers (finetune), column Multi-answer MSE

results.claim: On Multiply-divide, verbalized numbers only match the constant baseline in MSE and lose to the zero-shot answer logit.
results.table: Table 1, row Verbalized numbers (finetune), column Multiply-divide MSE
results.note: MAD for verbalized numbers on Multiply-divide is 19.0, worse than constant baseline 8.5

results.claim: Distribution shift in difficulty: GPT-3 median accuracy is much higher on the evaluation set than on training, so a calibrated model must raise its confidences.
Early stopping at about 2700 training examples is enough; more training does not improve generalization.
results.setup: verbalized numbers, Add-subtract, stop when per-sample training MSE flattens
results.quote: stop training after around n = 2700 examples

results.claim: Stochastic 50-shot prompting nearly matches finetuning on 10k datapoints, suggesting latent calibration features that examples only locate.
results.setup: Expected Value decoding, k random Add-subtract examples per query

limits: Only GPT-3 175B and only arithmetic; authors say future work should test other subject areas, formats (chat, long-form QA, forecasting) and other models.
Supervised finetuning rather than RL on a proper scoring rule; labels are sub-task accuracy, a noisy proxy per question.
Verbalized probability overfits training: the model only emits a number if that exact token appeared in training, giving lumpy calibration curves.
Underconfident on Multi-answer and no better than constant baseline on Multiply-divide; logit setups win there.
Single run, no seeds or intervals; many finetuning hyperparameters left at API defaults and unstated.
Calibration does not prove honesty; a model could imitate a calibrated person (authors concede).
